title: Elastic entitlements, preemption and backfill notes
body:
Purpose
---
Notes for an operational primitive we’re calling "elastic entitlements". Goal: give each tenant a soft, adjustable capacity entitlement across regions with deterministic preemption rules and a backfill mechanism that uses leftover capacity while respecting contract SLAs. This doc collects design options, control-plane APIs, metrics, rollout steps, and open questions.

Context and motivation
---
We currently route by tenant priorities and regional capacity buckets. During spikes noisy tenants either degrade everyone (flat shedding) or force expensive fallbacks. We want a model that:
- Explicitly encodes an entitlement per tenant (units = tokens per-second or per-concurrency)
- Lets control plane temporarily raise/lower entitlements using measurable signals (customer health, contract allowances, grace windows)
- Allows deterministic preemption so higher-contract tiers get immediate priority during scarcity
- Uses backfill windows to utilize spare capacity for lower tiers without risking SLA violations for higher tiers

Design goals
---
- Safety: never violate hard SLAs (dedicated/delivery contracts)
- Predictability: routing decisions should be explainable to customers and SREs
- Low-latency: decision path must be sub-ms in the data plane, control-plane decisions can be eventual (~1-5s)
- Observability: surface per-tenant entitlement, usage, preemptions, and backfill rates in Console
- Multi-region consistency: cross-region entitlements align with contract-scoped regions but must allow controlled spillover

Core primitives
---
1) Entitlement (E): static baseline from billing/contract (tokens/s or concurrent sessions).
2) BurstAllowance (B): short-lived, auto-decaying extra tokens granted for brief spikes (time-windowed).
3) CreditBalance (C): real-time gauge accrued by low usage; can be spent by tenant to sustain higher throughput later (optional).
4) BackfillSlot: ephemeral capacity available to lower-priority tenants when higher-priority tenants are not using their E+B. BackfillSlots have preemption tags.
5) LeaseToken: a lightweight lease that the data plane holds per-replica when serving a request that is billable against E/B/C/backfill. Leases are revocable.

Control-plane surface (sketch)
---
APIs (control plane -> data plane):
- PATCH /tenants/{id}/entitlement {baseline: number}  -- administrative update from billing/ops
- POST /tenants/{id}/burst-grant {amount: number, ttl_s: number, reason: string} -- human/automation grants
- POST /backfill-scheduler/run {region: string, window_s: number} -- opportunistic run to advertise slots
- POST /tenants/{id}/preempt {target_leases: number, reason: string} -- for emergency ejection from backfill
Data plane primitives:
- AcquireLease(tenant_id, units) -> {granted: bool, lease_id?: string, source: [E|B|C|Backfill], ttl_s}
- ReleaseLease(lease_id)
- ObserveUsage(tenant_id, tokens_used) -> emits usage metrics to control plane stream

Data-plane decision flow (per-request)
---
1) Check active hard-blockers (suspensions, region blacklists). If blocked -> reject with actionable code.
2) Attempt to consume from Entitlement (E). If available -> grant lease (source=E).
3) Else try BurstAllowance (B). If available -> grant (source=B).
4) Else check CreditBalance (C) if enabled and positive -> grant (source=C).
5) Else try BackfillSlot (best-effort, preemptable) -> grant (source=Backfill) and mark lease preemptable.
6) Else apply tenant-level throttle or return 429.
Note: Leases from Backfill can be preempted by control-plane Preempt calls or by a higher-priority request arriving; preemption should surface an error code that clients can interpret for retry/backoff.

Preemption semantics
---
- Preemption is last-in-first-out within backfill pool to avoid starving long-running tasks.
- A preempted lease receives a 100ms notice hook (best-effort) and a 503 with header X-Preempted: true so SDKs can record and fast-retry with jitter.
- When entitlement becomes available, control plane signals an async reclaim: backfill leases are rejected until reclaimed.

Backfill strategy
---
- Each region computes a backfill budget = max(0, available_capacity - safety_reserve). safety_reserve is a % of region capacity reserved for high-tier tenants (configurable per-region + per-tier).
- BackfillSlots are advertised in the control plane for up to window_s (e.g., 30s) and are mapped to specific model-serving pools to reduce cross-pool throttling surprises.
- Backfill usage is telemetry-tagged so billing/monitoring can attribute preemptions and effective cost savings.

Multi-region considerations
---
- Entitlements are primarily region-scoped. Contracts may specify multi-region entitlements (E_total) and per-region minima. Control plane computes regional allocations periodically and uses a leaky-bucket to permit short-term bursting across regions (spillover).
- Cross-region preemption: avoid synchronous cross-region evictions. Prefer local preemption first; if that doesn't free enough capacity, escalate to neighboring regions using priority-ordered list.
- Tradeoffs: synchronous global reconciliation gives strong correctness but adds latency; eventual reconciliation is simpler but can temporarily oversubscribe a customer (we add local safety reserves to avoid this).

Metrics and observable signals
---
- entitlement_allocated_{tenant,region} (tokens/s)
- entitlement_used_{tenant,region} (tokens/s)
- burst_grants_{tenant} (count, bytes)
- backfill_granted_{tenant,region} (tokens/s)
- preemption_events_{tenant,region} (count, reason)
- preemption_latency_ms (time between preempt request and eviction)
- backfill_success_rate (backfill->completed / backfill->preempted)
SLOs to track: % of time high-tier tenants served from E/B vs fallback, p95 latency for entitlement grants, percent of preemptions with <200ms notice.

Testing and rollout plan
---
1) Unit tests for AcquireLease semantics & preemption race invariants (simulated clocks).
2) Integration test harness: synthetic tenants with configurable traffic shapes (steady, spike, long-running) against a regional capacity emulator.
3) Canary in staging: enable Backfill for a single non-critical region and single low-tier customer (observe preemptions and metrics).
4) Gradual ramp: 5% of backfill capacity -> 20% -> 50% while monitoring backfill_success_rate and preemption complaints.
5) Beta: opt-in for a cohort of price-sensitive customers (lower cost when backfill used) + explicit billing tag.

Operational playbook (short)
---
- If preemption storms observed (preemption rate > threshold): increase safety_reserve by 10%, pause new burst grants, notify affected customers.
- If backfill SLA regressions: reduce backfill window_s and increase purge frequency.
- Tools needed: single-pane tenant entitlement dashboard, per-region backfill heatmap, preemption timeline viewer.

Known risks and mitigations
---
- Risk: noisy neighbor long-running work repeatedly gets preempted and retries, creating waste. Mitigation: add backoff budget and prefer LIFO granular preemption per-tenant.
- Risk: SDKs misinterpret preemptions as transient infra failures. Mitigation: add explicit error code + SDK best-practice doc and sample retry with jitter.
- Risk: accounting mismatch for backfill usage. Mitigation: require strong telemetry tagging and an offline reconciliation job that flags discrepancies.

Open questions
---
- Should CreditBalance (C) be billable? If yes, how priced relative to E/B?
- What is the right preemption-notice window for long-running GPU-backed sessions? 100ms is optimistic.
- How do we expose guarantees to customers in Console vs in contracts?

Immediate TODOs
---

- [ ] Add entitlement column to tenant table in billing DB (Liam).
- [ ] Draft SDK preemption recovery pattern doc (Ethan).
- [ ] Create staging chaos test that simulates sudden 3x spike for top 10 tenants (Maya).

Notes to reviewers
---
This is a working doc. Feedback desired on the preemption semantics and the multi-region spillover heuristics. If we like the LeaseToken model we can reuse it for Dedicated capacity isolation & for private deployments with minimal changes.
